chapter.name: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Iron Pillar of Delhi has stood in the open for over 1,600 years without rusting.
Reason (R): The pillar was dedicated to Vishnu, and its inscriptions celebrate the king's achievements.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the dedication to Vishnu and the praise of the king say nothing about why the iron does not rust; the chapter credits a thin protective layer formed by the special iron and oxygen from the air.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A tour guide at Mehrauli makes four remarks to a school group. Which remark does the chapter contradict?
questions.a: The chapter says the pillar was probably erected first in front of the Udayagiri caves in Madhya Pradesh and brought to Delhi a few centuries later, so it did move. The other three remarks are the guide's own facts.
o: The pillar has never left Mehrauli, where it was first put up
The pillar is over 1,600 years old and weighs about 6 tonnes
The pillar was dedicated to Vishnu and its inscription celebrates the king
The pillar was erected in the reign of Chandragupta II

questions.q: Isha says, 'The Iron Pillar can tell us about Chandragupta II's reign, because it was erected then and its inscription celebrates his achievements.' Do you agree? Explain with the chapter, and say what the pillar cannot tell us by itself.
questions.a: Yes, mostly. The chapter says the pillar was erected in his reign and that its inscription, which speaks of a king 'Chandra' identified with Chandragupta II, celebrates his achievements. But the pillar was probably moved from Udayagiri to Delhi, so its present place cannot show where he ruled, and an inscription that celebrates a king shows what was praised, not everything about his reign.
s: Verdict: agrees, with the reign and inscription as evidence
Notes the pillar was probably moved from Udayagiri, so its place is no proof of his territory
Notes that a celebrating inscription is one view of the reign

questions.q: Historians number kings of the same name by the chapter's reasoning: the 'II' in Chandragupta II was added because an earlier Chandragupta of the same family had lived. Suppose yet another Gupta king named Chandragupta ruled after Chandragupta II. Following the same reasoning, historians would write his name with the numeral ___.
questions.a: III

questions.q: A museum wall shows a Gupta family tree, earliest generation first. The chapter calls Chandragupta I the grandfather of Chandragupta II, Samudragupta his father, and Prabhavati Gupta his daughter. Which ordering of these four people is correct?
questions.a: Going by the relations the chapter gives: grandfather (Chandragupta I), then father (Samudragupta), then Chandragupta II, then his daughter (Prabhavati Gupta). Each wrong option moves one person into the wrong generation.
o: Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, Chandragupta II, Prabhavati Gupta
Samudragupta, Chandragupta I, Chandragupta II, Prabhavati Gupta
Chandragupta I, Chandragupta II, Samudragupta, Prabhavati Gupta
Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, Prabhavati Gupta, Chandragupta II

questions.q:
Read the statements about the rise of the Guptas.
1. When the Kushana Empire weakened by the 3rd century CE, the Gupta dynasty was the only new power to emerge.
2. Scientists believe the Iron Pillar is protected by a thin layer formed by the special iron used and oxygen from the air.
3. It is widely believed that the Guptas began as regional rulers near present-day Uttar Pradesh, though there are various theories of their origin.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: the chapter says new kingdoms emerged and the Gupta dynasty was the new actor among them, not the only one. Statements 2 and 3 repeat the chapter, including its 'widely believed' and 'various theories'.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A student writes: 'The Guptas defeated the Kushanas and took over their empire.' (a) State what the chapter says happened to the Kushana Empire by the 3rd century CE and who appeared as the new actor. (b) Which part of the student's sentence goes beyond the chapter, and why should a historian avoid it?
questions.a: (a) The Kushana Empire, spread over the north and northwest, started to weaken; new kingdoms emerged and the Gupta dynasty was the new actor. (b) 'Defeated and took over' goes beyond the chapter, which links the Guptas' rise to the Kushana weakening but never says they conquered the Kushanas. A historian should claim only what the sources support.
s: Part (a): Kushana weakening, new kingdoms, Gupta dynasty as the new actor
Part (b): picks 'defeated and took over' as unsupported and says claims must stay within the evidence

questions.q: A museum card describes a gold coin: on the front, Chandragupta I stands with his queen, Kumaradevi; on the back, a seated goddess is identified as Lakshmi. A student lists four statements about the coin. Which one cannot be read off the coin itself and needs other evidence?
questions.a: The coin shows the king, the queen, the goddess and the gold. That the king's strategic alliances helped him consolidate power is something the chapter tells us about him; the coin alone does not prove it.
o: His strategic alliances helped him consolidate power
He is shown together with his queen, Kumaradevi
A seated goddess identified as Lakshmi is on the reverse
The coin was struck in gold, not in a cheaper metal

questions.q: Differentiate between Chandragupta I and Chandragupta II on two points each, drawn from the chapter.
questions.a: Chandragupta I: the grandfather, remembered for coins and alliances that helped the early expansion. Chandragupta II: his grandson, also called Vikramaditya, a devotee of Vishnu, in whose reign the Iron Pillar was erected and the arts flourished.
s: Two correct points about Chandragupta I
Two correct points about Chandragupta II, kept separate

questions.q:
Match each description with the person it fits.
Column A: 1. The king whose name on a Delhi pillar is read as 'Chandra'  2. The king remembered for coins and strategic alliances, who gave his name to a later king  3. A ruler of an earlier dynasty, not to be confused with the pillar's king  4. The father of the pillar's king
Column B: a. Samudragupta  b. Chandragupta Maurya  c. Chandragupta I  d. Chandragupta II
questions.a: The pillar's 'Chandra' is Chandragupta II; the coins-and-alliances king is Chandragupta I (his grandfather); the earlier dynasty is the Mauryas, so Chandragupta Maurya; his father is Samudragupta.

questions.q: The science club of a Jaipur school wants to copy the Iron Pillar's protection on a garden gate. Going only by how the chapter explains the pillar, which plan follows that explanation?
questions.a: The chapter says the protection is a thin layer made by the special iron used together with oxygen from the air. So the gate needs that iron and must be open to air; weight, dedication and a sealed case do not supply the layer.
o: Make the gate from the same special iron and keep it open to air
Make the gate as heavy as 6 tonnes so that rain cannot reach the metal
Engrave a dedication to Vishnu on the gate, as on the pillar
Seal the gate in an airtight case so that no air touches the iron

questions.q: (a) Name the two kinds of source in this part of the chapter that tell us about Gupta rulers: one carved on the Mehrauli pillar and one struck for Chandragupta I. (b) Which of the two gave historians a name that still had to be identified, and how did the chapter resolve it?
questions.a: (a) An inscription (on the iron pillar) and a coin (of Chandragupta I with his queen). (b) The pillar's inscription, which speaks only of a king 'Chandra'; this has been identified with Chandragupta II, not Chandragupta Maurya.
s: Part (a): inscription and coin
Part (b): the inscription's 'Chandra' identified with Chandragupta II

questions.q: The chapter says art, architecture, literature and science flourished 'particularly during the time of Chandragupta II'. A student concludes that these fields did not exist before him. (a) Which word in the chapter's sentence shows the flaw? (b) Give one chapter detail showing that the empire's strength was being built before Chandragupta II.
questions.a: (a) 'Particularly' marks a peak within a longer flowering; it does not say nothing existed earlier. (b) Chandragupta I played a crucial role in the early expansion of the empire and is remembered for coins and strategic alliances that helped him consolidate power.
s: Part (a): 'particularly' marks a peak, not a beginning
Part (b): Chandragupta I's early expansion, coins or alliances

questions.q: 'The Iron Pillar is both a marvel of science and a document of history.' Justify this statement using the chapter.
questions.a: Science: over 1,600 years old, about 6 tonnes, unrusted because of the special iron and a thin protective layer, which shows advanced metallurgy. History: it was erected in Chandragupta II's reign, dedicated to Vishnu, its inscription names 'Chandra' and celebrates the king's achievements, and it was probably moved from Udayagiri. So it tells us both what ancient craftsmen could do and who was ruling.
s: Science: age, weight and rust-resistance explained
History: reign, Vishnu, inscription and the move from Udayagiri
Draws the two together in a conclusion

questions.q: Piya says, 'The chapter says the Guptas began as regional rulers near present-day Uttar Pradesh.' Qadir adds, 'So historians all agree where the Guptas began, and the matter is closed.' Test both statements against the chapter.
questions.a: Piya is partly right: the chapter says it is widely believed that they emerged near present-day Uttar Pradesh as regional rulers, so her sentence turns a belief into a fact. Qadir is wrong: the chapter says there are various theories on the origin. The safe statement: the widely held view places them near present-day Uttar Pradesh, but the origin is not settled.
s: Piya: partly right, because the chapter says 'widely believed', not certain
Qadir: wrong, because the chapter mentions various theories
Gives a safe, corrected statement of the origin

questions.q:
A Pune school builds a three-card trail on the Iron Pillar. Card 1: 'Over 1,600 years old; about 6 tonnes; stands at Mehrauli, Delhi.' Card 2: 'Inscription speaks of a king Chandra; pillar dedicated to Vishnu.' Card 3: 'Probably first erected in front of the Udayagiri caves, Madhya Pradesh; brought to Delhi a few centuries later.' Anaya says, 'Card 3 means the pillar is not really from Gupta times.' Dev says, 'Cards 1 and 2 are enough; visitors will see Delhi and know the Guptas ruled there.'
(a) Is Anaya right? Use the chapter.
(b) A visitor reads Card 2 and says 'Chandra is Chandragupta Maurya.' Give the chapter's correction and say what Card 2 should add.
(c) Which card protects visitors from Dev's conclusion, and how?
(d) Space allows only two cards. Which two would you keep? Name what visitors would lose.
questions.a: (a) No. The chapter says the pillar was erected in Chandragupta II's reign and brought to Delhi a few centuries later; moving it changes its place, not its date. (b) 'Chandra' is identified with Chandragupta II of the Gupta dynasty, not Chandragupta Maurya; Card 2 should add that identification. (c) Card 3: since the pillar was moved from Madhya Pradesh, its Delhi site is not proof that the Guptas ruled Delhi. (d) Keep Cards 2 and 3 for an accurate story and lose the science of the unrusted iron, or keep Cards 1 and 2 and risk the Delhi misreading; either choice needs its loss named.
s: Part (a): no; erected in his reign, moved later; place is not date
Part (b): Chandragupta II not Maurya; Card 2 adds the identification
Part (c): Card 3; the pillar was moved, so Delhi is no proof of Gupta rule there
Part (d): a pair chosen with its loss named

questions.q: Write a three-sentence museum caption for the Iron Pillar. Each sentence must rest on the chapter, and one sentence must state something the pillar does NOT prove. Explain in one line why you placed each sentence.
questions.a: Sample: 'This pillar has stood in the open for over 1,600 years; the chapter credits a thin layer formed by its special iron and oxygen from the air. It was erected in the reign of Chandragupta II and dedicated to Vishnu, and its inscription celebrates the king. It probably stood first near the Udayagiri caves, so its place in Delhi does not show that the Guptas ruled Delhi.' Each sentence is a chapter fact; the last one limits what a visitor may infer.
s: A sentence on age and protection from the chapter
A sentence on reign, dedication or inscription from the chapter
A sentence stating what the pillar does not prove, with the reason (it was moved)

questions.q: The chapter says the Kushana decline set the stage for 'a fresh period of consolidation'. Analyse how the early Guptas, up to Chandragupta II, built on that opening.
questions.a: The Kushana Empire weakened and new kingdoms emerged. The Guptas rose from near present-day Uttar Pradesh as regional rulers. Chandragupta I helped early expansion with coins and strategic alliances, laying a foundation. By Chandragupta II, art, architecture, literature and science were flourishing and the pillar was erected. Each step moved from a regional power to a remarkable empire.
s: Kushana weakening gave the opening
Guptas begin as regional rulers near present-day Uttar Pradesh
Chandragupta I: coins and alliances as foundation
Chandragupta II: flourishing of fields and the pillar
Links the stages into a clear line of growth

questions.q:
The history club of a Lucknow school plans one large banner for its 'Guptas begin' wall. Note 1: 'By the 3rd century CE the Kushana Empire, spread over the north and northwest, began to weaken, and new kingdoms emerged.' Note 2: 'The Guptas are widely believed to have begun near present-day Uttar Pradesh; there are various theories.' Note 3: 'Chandragupta I laid foundations through coins and alliances; art, architecture, literature and science flourished particularly under Chandragupta II.'
(a) Which note explains why a new dynasty could rise when it did, and which phrase does the work?
(b) What would a visitor wrongly believe if Note 2 were shortened to 'The Guptas were rulers from Uttar Pradesh'?
(c) Note 3 names two kings with one name. Show how a visitor can tell them apart using the chapter.
(d) Only one note can go on the banner. Choose one and state what the wall loses.
questions.a: (a) Note 1; 'started to weaken' and 'new kingdoms emerged' explain the opening. (b) That the origin is certain and settled, when the chapter says it is only widely believed and that theories differ. (c) The numeral: historians added II because an earlier Chandragupta, his grandfather, came first; Chandragupta I is the one of coins and alliances. (d) Note 1 gives the cause but drops the people; Note 3 gives the people and the peak but drops why the rise was possible; Note 2 is the least informative. Any choice with its loss named.
s: Part (a): Note 1; the Kushana weakening and new kingdoms
Part (b): would believe the origin is certain, losing 'widely believed' and the competing theories
Part (c): numeral II from the earlier Chandragupta, the grandfather; I is the coins-and-alliances king
Part (d): one note chosen and the loss named

questions.q: (a) The Iron Pillar has stood outdoors for over 1,600 years, while the chapter says a bicycle left in the rain would show rust within about a year. At least how many times longer has the pillar lasted? (b) A student concludes that all outdoor iron lasts that many times longer than a bicycle. What does the chapter's explanation say is missing in the bicycle's case?
questions.a: (a) 1,600 / 1 = 1,600 times. (b) The pillar is protected by a thin layer formed by the special iron used and oxygen from the air; the bicycle's ordinary iron is not described as forming such a layer, so the comparison cannot be generalised to all iron.
s: Part (a): about 1,600 times
Part (b): the protection comes from the special iron forming a layer; ordinary iron is not shown to do so

questions.q: True or False: 'The thin layer that protects the Iron Pillar would also protect an ordinary iron bicycle left in the rain for a year.' Give the verdict, then the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the layer forms from the special iron used together with oxygen from the air, and that an ordinary bicycle left out for a year would soon show rust.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the layer depends on the special iron; the bicycle would rust

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Samudragupta fought many wars, defeating kings and expanding his empire.
Reason (R): According to Harisena, his ambition was to be dharani-bandha, 'to unify the Earth'.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The chapter says that 'to this end', the aim of unifying the Earth, he fought many wars. R gives the aim behind the wars in A, so it explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Meera wants evidence for Harisena's claim that Samudragupta supported the arts that does NOT come from Harisena's own inscription. Which source in the chapter should she use?
questions.a: A coin the king minted that shows him seated and playing the veena is independent of the inscription and points to the arts. The coin with the queen belongs to Chandragupta I, the horse coin recalls an ashvamedha yajna, and the Vishnu Purana's list is about regions.
o: A coin showing him playing the veena, Lakshmi on the reverse
A coin showing Chandragupta I with his queen Kumaradevi
A coin showing a sacrificial horse and a queen with a fly whisk
The Vishnu Purana's list of Anuganga, Prayaga, Saketa and Magadha

questions.q: Two kings are defeated by Samudragupta. King A's kingdom is taken over; King B is reinstated and offers tribute. (a) Which of them sits on a throne after the campaign? (b) Using the chapter's reasoning about his army, give one benefit to Samudragupta of keeping King B on the throne instead of taking his kingdom over.
questions.a: (a) King B. (b) Tributary kings could be asked to provide supplies for the huge army (soldiers, elephants, horses, cooks and support staff), and tribute flowed to him without his ruling that land directly.
s: Part (a): King B
Part (b): tributary kings could supply the army, or tribute without direct rule

questions.q: After a campaign, a defeated king keeps his throne but must send Samudragupta a regular share of his wealth. The chapter's word for such a king, who offers payment while still ruling, is a ___ king.
questions.a: tributary

questions.q: Pooja says, 'Samudragupta was a patron of the arts as well as a warrior.' Do you agree? Support your answer with two pieces of evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. Warrior: he fought many wars and defeated kings. Patron: Harisena wrote that he supported art, learning and trade, and one of his coins shows him playing the veena. The claim is supported by both sources.
s: Verdict: agrees
Warrior evidence: many wars and defeated kings
Patron evidence: Prashasti on art, learning and trade, or the veena coin

questions.q: A quiz-master reads out four outcomes for a king defeated by Samudragupta. Which outcome is described by the word 'tributary' in the chapter?
questions.a: A tributary king was reinstated and offered tribute. A king whose kingdom was taken over lost his throne to the empire, and a king who submitted without protest acted out of fear of his might; neither is the tribute arrangement.
o: He is reinstated and offers tribute to Samudragupta
He loses his kingdom, which is taken over by Samudragupta
He submits without protest, fearing the might of Samudragupta
He is made a soldier in the Gupta army and loses his land

questions.q:
A heritage-trail officer marks the Vishnu Purana's key regions on a present-day map. Match each Purana name with how the chapter identifies it.
Column A: 1. Anuganga  2. Prayaga  3. Saketa  4. Magadha
Column B: a. The middle-Gangetic basin  b. Present-day Prayagraj  c. Ayodhya  d. Approximately Bihar
questions.a: The chapter glosses Anuganga as the middle-Gangetic basin, Prayaga as present-day Prayagraj, Saketa as Ayodhya and Magadha as approximately Bihar. Two of the four are regions, not city points.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the sources for Samudragupta.
1. Many defeated kings were reinstated and offered tribute, while others submitted without protest.
2. The Prayaga Prashasti praises Chandragupta II, who was the father of Samudragupta.
3. One of the coins Samudragupta minted portrays him as a veena player.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 is false: the Prashasti praises Samudragupta, who was the father of Chandragupta II, so the relationship is reversed. Statements 1 and 3 are in the chapter.
o: 1 and 3 only
2 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: 'No single source tells the whole story of Samudragupta and his empire.' Justify this statement using the Prayaga Prashasti, the coins and the Vishnu Purana.
questions.a: Prashasti: written by the court poet Harisena, it tells of his ambition to unify the Earth, many wars, reinstated kings and support for art, learning and trade. Coins: one shows him playing the veena and another recalls an ashvamedha yajna, which add the arts and imperial ambition. Vishnu Purana: names Anuganga, Prayaga, Saketa, Magadha and 'surrounding regions', but at its peak the empire was larger. Each source adds something the others do not, so they need to be read together.
s: Prashasti: what it tells
Coins: what they add
Purana: regions named and the larger peak extent
Conclusion: sources need to be combined

questions.q: The Prashasti says many defeated kings were reinstated and offered tribute. Separately, the chapter reasons that moving a huge army needed supplies, so tributary kings 'must have been asked' to provide. Which link between the two statements is the chapter's own reasoning?
questions.a: Because the defeated kings had been reinstated and were paying tribute to Samudragupta, they were the natural people to ask to provide for his army. The other options reverse the order or bring in claims the chapter does not make.
o: Reinstated kings owed him tribute, so they could supply the army
Kings were reinstated only after they had supplied his army first
His army fed itself, so tribute was never needed from reinstated kings
Only kings whose kingdoms were taken over supplied the army

questions.q:
A Bhopal teacher builds a classroom model from the chapter. Of 24 kings Samudragupta faced, 9 had their kingdoms taken over, 10 were reinstated and offered tribute, and the rest submitted without protest.
(a) How many kings submitted without protest?
(b) What percentage of the 24 lost their kingdoms?
(c) Which group does the chapter's reasoning about supplying the army rely on, and how many of the 24 are in it in this model?
(d) Raj says, '15 of the 24 kingdoms were not taken over, so Samudragupta was not really a conqueror.' Judge Raj's claim using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 24 - 9 - 10 = 5. (b) 9/24 = 37.5%. (c) The tributary kings, those reinstated who paid tribute: 10. (d) Raj is wrong. Not taking over a kingdom is not the same as not conquering: the reinstated kings had been defeated first, and the chapter says that to unify the Earth he fought many wars, defeating kings; some kings submitted only because they feared his might.
s: Part (a): 5
Part (c): tributary (reinstated) kings; 10
Part (d): claim rejected; reinstated kings were first defeated, and he fought many wars

questions.q: Read the two coins as evidence: one shows Samudragupta with a veena, another shows a sacrificial horse. What does each tell us about him, and what do they show together?
questions.a: The veena coin shows him as a patron of art. The horse coin recalls an ashvamedha yajna, which ambitious kings performed to build empires. Together they show a warrior-king who also loved the arts.
s: Veena coin: patron of art
Horse coin: ashvamedha and imperial ambition
Combines the two into one picture of the king

questions.q: In a classroom model of the march, there are 50 elephants needing 200 kg of fodder each per day and 400 horses needing 10 kg each per day. (a) What is the total fodder needed for a 20-day march? (b) Whom does the chapter suggest the army relied on for such supplies, and why does that arrangement fit a ruler who had reinstated defeated kings?
questions.a: (a) Elephants 50 x 200 = 10,000 kg; horses 400 x 10 = 4,000 kg; 14,000 kg a day; x 20 = 280,000 kg. (b) The tributary kings; reinstated kings paid tribute, so asking them to supply the army used the arrangement already in place.
s: Part (a): 280,000 kg
Part (b): tributary kings, because reinstated kings already owed tribute

questions.q: A student writes in a test: 'Samudragupta's kingdom became rich and successful because he took over every neighbouring kingdom.' According to Harisena's account in the chapter, which cause does it actually give for the kingdom's richness?
questions.a: Harisena wrote that the king supported art, learning and trade, making his kingdom rich and successful. Taking over kingdoms and tribute are real parts of the story but are not the cause he gives for the richness.
o: His support for art, learning and trade
The tribute paid by reinstated kings
His many wars and taking over of kingdoms
His ashvamedha yajna and its special coins

questions.q: Rohan makes three claims. C1: 'Samudragupta wished to unify the Earth.' C2: 'Magadha was among the key regions of the Gupta dynasty.' C3: 'Samudragupta was portrayed as a veena player.' (a) Name the kind of source (inscription, literary text or coin) that the chapter uses for each claim. (b) Which claim depends on a source not made for or by the king's own circle, and why?
questions.a: (a) C1: the Prayaga Prashasti, an inscription; C2: the Vishnu Purana, a literary text; C3: a coin. (b) C2, because the Vishnu Purana is a literary text and not a pillar inscription by the court poet or a coin minted by the king.
s: Part (a): inscription, literary text, coin in that order
Part (b): C2, the Purana, which is not the court poet's inscription or the king's coin

questions.q:
A Prayagraj museum has room for one headline source on its panel 'Samudragupta: warrior or patron?'. Source P is the Prayaga Prashasti, written by his court poet Harisena, which tells of wars, reinstated kings, and support for art, learning and trade. Source Q is the coin he minted that shows him playing the veena. Source R is a coin with a sacrificial horse, recalling an ashvamedha yajna.
(a) Which of P, Q and R speaks to both sides of the title, and what does it say on each side?
(b) P was written by his court poet and Q was minted by the king himself. Why should neither be treated as a neutral account?
(c) Which side does R support, and what did the chapter say ambitious kings hoped to gain from the yajna?
(d) Choose the headline source and state the cost of your choice.
questions.a: (a) P: wars and defeated kings on the warrior side; support for art, learning and trade on the patron side. (b) Both come from the king's own circle (his court poet and his own mint), so they show how he wished to be seen. (c) The warrior or ambitious side; kings performed the yajna to build mighty empires and leave a legacy. (d) P is the most informative single source but is a court poet's praise; Q or R would be the king's own image yet show only one side. Any choice with its cost named.
s: Part (a): P; wars and defeated kings, and art, learning and trade
Part (b): both are from the king's circle, so they show his chosen image
Part (c): the ambition side; mighty empire and legacy
Part (d): a source chosen and its cost named

questions.q: Meera says, 'The chapter says Samudragupta took over the kingdom of every king he defeated.' Do you agree? Explain with the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says he defeated kings and took over their kingdoms, but many defeated kings were reinstated and offered tribute, and others submitted without protest. So 'every' is wrong; taking over was one outcome among three.
s: Verdict: no, 'every' over-claims
Reinstated kings who paid tribute
Kings who submitted without protest

questions.q: Compare the three ways Samudragupta dealt with the kings he met: taking kingdoms over, reinstating kings who paid tribute, and kings who submitted without protest. Analyse how these helped him build an empire.
questions.a: Some kingdoms were taken over, which added land directly to the empire. Others were reinstated and paid tribute, which brought wealth and supplies without ruling them directly. Some kings submitted at once, fearing his might, so no war was needed. Together, force and fear produced a large empire and tributary kings could also provide for his huge army.
s: Taking over described
Reinstating with tribute described
Peaceful submission described
Analysis: how each added to the empire
Link to supplying the army

questions.q: The book asks, 'Why do you think kings chose to proclaim their achievements in the form of inscriptions?' (a) Name one achievement of Samudragupta that Harisena's inscription proclaims. (b) Give one reason, in your own words, why a king would have such achievements cut in stone for the public.
questions.a: (a) Any one: he fought many wars and defeated kings; he supported art, learning and trade. (b) A reasoned inference, for example: stone lasts for a long time and many people can see it, so the achievements are remembered and the king's power is announced. The book leaves this question for the reader.
s: Part (a): one achievement from the Prashasti
Part (b): a sensible reason such as lasting, public record

questions.q: Explain why the Vishnu Purana alone cannot be used to say how large the Gupta Empire was at its peak.
questions.a: It names only key regions (Anuganga, Prayaga, Saketa, Magadha and the surrounding regions). At its peak the empire covered most of north and west India with parts of central and east India, which is larger. So a single source gives only part of the picture and others are needed.
s: States what the Purana lists
States the larger peak extent
Concludes more than one source is needed

questions.q: True or False: 'The Prayaga Prashasti comes from outside Samudragupta's court, so it is a neutral account of his rule.' Give the verdict, then the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says it was written by the court poet Harisena, so it comes from the king's own court and praises him; it is one view that needs other sources such as coins and the Vishnu Purana.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the author was the court poet, so it is a view from inside the court

questions.q: Faxian says people 'have no need to register households or attend to officials'. Divya concludes that the Gupta state collected nothing from ordinary people. Which line of the same excerpt weakens her conclusion?
o: Farmers of royal land pay a portion of their grain
The king's guards and attendants have salaries
The lanes are kept in good order
Heads of Vaishya families establish houses for charity
questions.a: Paying a portion of grain by farmers of royal land is a payment to the king, so the state did collect from some people. Salaries, tidy lanes and charity houses are real lines of the excerpt but say nothing about collection.

questions.q: The dates printed with Faxian's record are AD 399 to AD 414. The years between its first and last date number ___.
Divya's cousin reads the Faxian excerpt and says, 'So the king himself ran the houses for charity and medicines.' Which correction does the excerpt support?
questions.a: The excerpt says heads of Vaishya families establish houses for charity and medicines, where the poor, orphans and sick are cared for. It does not give the king that role; the other options name people the excerpt links to other duties or to nothing.
o: The heads of Vaishya families did, not the king
Foreign merchants alone set them up, not Gupta families
The king's guards and attendants ran them for a salary
Priests set them up from the income of land grants

questions.q: True or False: 'Faxian's remark that farmers of royal land pay a portion of their grain fits the chapter's statement that land tax was the main source of Gupta revenue.' Give the verdict, then the reason.
questions.a: True. Paying a portion of grain from royal land is a payment on land, and the chapter names land tax as the primary source of Gupta revenue, so the two accounts are consistent with each other. This is an inference: the excerpt does not use the words 'land tax'.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the grain payment on royal land is consistent with land tax as the main revenue source

questions.q: Show that Faxian's excerpt, taken alone, cannot tell us what fraction of their grain the farmers of royal land paid.
questions.a: The excerpt says only that they pay 'a portion of their grain'; no fraction is given. The chapter also names land tax as the main revenue but gives no rate. So the fraction cannot be found from these; a historian would have to turn to other sources, as the chapter advises, and compare them.
s: Notes the wording 'a portion' gives no number
Notes the chapter's revenue account also gives no rate
Concludes other sources must be compared, and the answer cannot be worked out here

questions.q:
A Coimbatore library displays 'A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms (AD 399-414)', translated by J. Legge, and has room for exactly two cards. Card 1: 'Farmers of royal land pay a portion of their grain; the king's guards and attendants have salaries.' Card 2: 'Heads of Vaishya families set up houses for charity and medicines.' Card 3: 'Elsewhere in his travelogue Faxian describes the harsh treatment of the chandalas.' Card 4: 'Historians corroborate a traveller's account with other sources.'
(a) Which of the four cards do not come from the excerpt's own lines, and where do they come from?
(b) Find the span of the record's dates in years. Taking the Gupta Empire as flourishing across the whole of the 3rd to 6th centuries (400 years), what percentage of that period does the record cover? Give your answer to two decimal places.
(c) What does your answer to (b) suggest about treating the excerpt as a picture of the whole period?
(d) Choose the two cards to display and state what visitors will miss.
questions.a: (a) Card 3 comes from elsewhere in Faxian's travelogue (the chapter mentions it); Card 4 is the chapter's own advice on method. (b) 414 - 399 = 15 years; 15/400 = 3.75%. (c) The record covers only a small slice of the period, so the excerpt is one snapshot and cannot by itself describe the whole age. (d) Any pair with its loss named: for example Cards 1 and 3 give governance and a missing side but drop the charity picture; Cards 3 and 4 give the cautions but drop the content of the account.
s: Part (a): Cards 3 and 4; travelogue elsewhere, chapter's method
Part (b): 15 years, 3.75%
Part (c): a small slice of the period, so one snapshot only
Part (d): a pair chosen and the loss named

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Faxian's travelogue has survived to this day.
Reason (R): Faxian was a Chinese traveller who visited India in the early 5th century CE.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true. Who he was and when he came do not explain why the text has survived, so R is not the explanation.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Faxian writes of 'wealthy Vaishya elders and foreign merchants' and of heads of Vaishya families who establish houses for charity and medicines. (a) What does the bracketed note in the chapter say the Vaishya were? (b) Give one inference that links these two lines, and say what the excerpt does not tell us that limits that inference.
questions.a: (a) Merchants or traders. (b) Inference: wealth from trade allowed some families to fund charity houses. Limit: the excerpt does not say where their money came from, so the link is an inference, not a statement.
s: Part (a): merchants or traders
Part (b): a reasoned link between wealth and charity, with the missing evidence named

questions.q: A Class 7 teacher asks students to list conclusions that the quoted Faxian excerpt ALONE can support. Which conclusion cannot be drawn from the excerpt alone?
o: Chandalas were treated harshly and lived outside the cities
The king's guards and attendants were paid salaries by the king
Farmers of royal land paid a share of their grain to the king
Vaishya family heads ran houses for charity and medicines
questions.a: The harsh treatment of the chandalas is reported elsewhere in his travelogue, not in the quoted lines, so the excerpt alone cannot support it. Salaries, a share of grain and charity houses are all lines of the excerpt.

questions.q: Faxian's excerpt says farmers of royal land pay a portion of their grain, and that the king's guards and attendants have salaries. Mehul says, 'Put together, these lines suggest the state's staff were paid out of what it collected.' How should a historian treat Mehul's sentence?
questions.a: It is an inference: the excerpt states the two facts separately, and the chapter's account of revenue (land tax, used for administration) fits it. A historian marks it as a reasoned link, not as something the excerpt says.
o: As a reasonable inference that the excerpt does not itself state
As a fact that the excerpt states in so many words
As false, because the excerpt says people need not register households
As false, because Vaishya heads paid the salaries

questions.q: 'Faxian's account is valuable, but it cannot be read alone.' Justify this statement.
questions.a: It is valuable because he travelled extensively, recorded his own observations of governance and society, and his travelogue has survived. His excerpt tells us about taxes in grain, salaried guards, rich cities and charity houses. But it reflects only his perspective at one time and a limited part of society, and he himself reports harsh treatment of chandalas. Different historians may read it differently, so they check with other sources.
s: Value: travelled widely and recorded observations
Details from the excerpt
Limits: one writer, one time, one part of society
Chandalas as evidence of a missing side
Conclusion: compare multiple sources

questions.q: A student says, 'Faxian came to India to study Gupta governance, so his remarks on taxes and salaries are his main findings.' (a) Name the three aims the chapter gives for his journey. (b) Why does this make the student's claim go beyond the chapter?
questions.a: (a) To visit sacred Buddhist sites, learn from renowned Indian scholars and collect manuscripts of Buddhist texts. (b) Governance is not among the stated aims; the chapter says he observed governance along the way while travelling, so his remarks on it are observations, not the purpose of his journey.
s: Part (a): sacred sites, scholars, manuscripts
Part (b): governance was an observation made on the way, not a stated aim

questions.q:
Read the statements about Faxian's account.
1. Faxian set out on a pilgrimage and recorded his observations of culture, governance and society for the people of his homeland.
2. In the excerpt, it is the heads of Vaishya families, not the king, who establish houses for charity and medicines.
3. Elsewhere in his travelogue Faxian describes the harsh treatment of the chandalas, who lived inside the city among the wealthy Vaishya elders.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 3 is false: the chapter says the chandalas were regarded as outcastes and lived outside the city limits. Statements 1 and 2 follow the chapter and the excerpt.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: Mohit says, 'Faxian travelled extensively across India, so his excerpt shows how the whole of Gupta society lived.' Do you agree? Explain with the chapter.
questions.a: Only partly. It is true that he travelled extensively and recorded governance and society. But the chapter says such an excerpt reflects only the writer's perspective, at one point in time and for a limited portion of society, and Faxian himself reports harsh treatment of the chandalas elsewhere. So it shows a part, not the whole.
s: Verdict: partly right, not the whole
Credits his wide travel and recording
Limits: one writer, one time, a limited portion of society

questions.q: A teacher asks students to underline the one line of Faxian's excerpt that records the writer's own judgement rather than something he could count or see. Which line should they underline?
questions.a: 'Happy' is the writer's own reading of people's feelings. Grain paid by farmers, salaries of guards and attendants, and houses for charity set up by Vaishya heads are things an observer could see or be told and record.
o: The people are numerous and happy
Those who farm royal land pay a portion of their grain
The king's guards and attendants have salaries
Heads of Vaishya families establish houses for charity and medicines

questions.q: A historian wants to corroborate Faxian's line that farmers of royal land pay a portion of their grain. Write two questions she could ask, and for each name a statement from the chapter's own account of the Gupta state that could answer it.
questions.a: Sample: (1) Did the Guptas collect land tax? The chapter says the primary source of Gupta revenue was land tax. (2) Were land arrangements recorded for tax purposes? The chapter says land grants were inscribed on copper plates to keep accurate records and ensure proper tax collection.
s: A sound question with a matching chapter statement
A second, different question with a matching chapter statement

questions.q: Faxian's excerpt says: 'The people are numerous and happy [...] they have no need to register households or attend to officials. [...] Those who farm royal land pay a portion of their grain. [...] The king's guards and attendants have salaries [...] Heads of Vaishya families establish houses for charity and medicines [...] the poor, orphans and the sick are cared for.' Draw three different conclusions about Gupta society from these lines, each tied to a line. Then say what a historian must do before accepting them.
questions.a: Prosperity or contentment: 'numerous and happy'. Light administration and land tax: no need to register households, and farmers of royal land pay a portion of grain. Salaried staff: guards and attendants have salaries. Welfare: Vaishya heads run charity and medicine houses for the poor, orphans and sick. A historian must compare with other sources and perspectives, because one traveller's excerpt reflects only his own view at one time.
s: First conclusion tied to a line
Second conclusion tied to a line
Third conclusion tied to a line
Compare with other sources and perspectives
Limits of one account or varied interpretations

questions.q:
At a Kolkata school, a debate is held on the motion 'Faxian's travelogue is a good source for the Gupta age.' Team For says he travelled extensively, observed governance and society first-hand, and his record has survived. Team Against says the textbook passage describes only the wealthy cities and says nothing of the chandalas, whom the chapter says he describes harshly elsewhere.
(a) Which group does Team Against say the passage leaves out, and where does the chapter place that group's lives?
(b) Team Against also claims the passage describes only the cities. Test this claim using two lines about other people in the excerpt.
(c) Which fact from the chapter's account of Gupta revenue is consistent with the excerpt's line on grain from royal land?
(d) The judge awards the point to the team that best deals with the other side's strongest fact. Which team does so more convincingly, and how?
questions.a: (a) The chandalas, outcastes who lived outside the city limits. (b) The claim is partly wrong: the excerpt also mentions farmers of royal land paying grain and the king's guards and attendants with salaries, who are not city merchants. (c) Land tax was the primary source of revenue. (d) A choice with a reason: Team For can answer Team Against's strongest fact by agreeing the excerpt has limits and by corroborating with other sources; Team Against's strongest fact (the omitted group and one writer's view) is a limit that Team For must accept, but it does not make the source useless.
s: Part (a): chandalas; outside the city limits
Part (b): claim partly wrong; farmers of royal land and salaried guards or attendants
Part (c): land tax as primary revenue
Part (d): a team chosen by how it handles the other side's strongest fact

questions.q: Imagine a traveller from another country visits your town today. Write three lines of her record, one about taxes or pay, one about how the poor are cared for, and one limitation of her view. Base the form on Faxian's excerpt.
questions.a: Any three lines of the right kinds, for example: shopkeepers pay a share of earnings; clinics treat the poor free; I saw only the market streets and not every home. A good answer shows that a single traveller sees only part.
s: A line about taxes or salaries
A line about care for the poor
A line that admits the limitation of one visitor's view

questions.q: Faxian's quoted excerpt says the people are 'numerous and happy' and the lanes 'are kept in good order'. (a) Which group does the chapter say he elsewhere describes as outcastes living outside the city limits? (b) How does leaving this group out of the excerpt limit what a historian may conclude from it?
questions.a: (a) The chandalas. (b) The excerpt covers only a limited portion of society, so 'happy' cannot be taken to describe everyone; the chandalas' harsh treatment shows a missing side.
s: Part (a): the chandalas
Part (b): the excerpt shows only a limited portion, so its picture cannot be applied to everyone

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Indian Ocean trade network connected Indian ports to distant markets.
Reason (R): Land tax was the primary source of Gupta revenue.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. Land tax shows what the state collected at home; it says nothing about why ports were linked across the ocean.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A historian finds an inscription in which an earlier ruler is called 'rajan' and a coin in which a later Gupta ruler is called 'chakravartin' and 'samrat'. Going by the chapter, what can she safely conclude from the titles alone?
questions.a: The chapter says the later titles reflected a claim to supreme authority and a superiority over earlier rulers with simpler titles. A title is a claim; it does not prove the later ruler held more land or defeated the earlier one.
o: The later ruler claimed a higher authority than the earlier one
The later ruler held a larger territory than the earlier one
The later ruler had defeated the earlier ruler in battle
The earlier ruler belonged to the Gupta dynasty

questions.q: Sneha says, 'The Guptas ran the whole empire from one central authority: local rulers, priests and chieftains were given no land and no control.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says that instead of controlling everything from a central authority, the Guptas divided the empire into provinces and granted land to local rulers, priests and chieftains, recorded on copper plates. This helped tax collection and still gave local leaders some control over their regions.
s: Verdict: no, the claim reverses the chapter
Provinces and land grants to local rulers, priests and chieftains
Effect: tax collection and some local control

questions.q: Suppose, as in the chapter, a Vakataka prince dies early and Prabhavati Gupta becomes regent. The elder of his sons is 11 years old, and in this imagined case a Vakataka king governs from the age of 18. She would be regent for the elder son for ___ years.

In an imagined Gupta province with yearly revenue of 1,000 units, land tax brings 400, fines 250, taxes on mines and irrigation 200, and taxes on trade and crafts 150. Rohit says, 'Land tax cannot be the primary source here, because it is under half the total.' How does the chapter's description of land tax help to judge him?
questions.a: The chapter calls land tax the primary source of revenue, meaning the main one. At 400 units it is larger than each of the other three groups, so it is primary even though it is below 500. Rohit confuses primary with a majority.
o: He is wrong, because 400 units is larger than each of the other sources
He is right, because a primary source must supply more than half
He is wrong, because fines and trade together bring in less than 400
He is right, because the other sources together bring in 600 units

questions.q:
Match each piece of evidence with the conclusion the chapter draws from it.
Column A: 1. Titles such as samrat and chakravartin  2. Copper-plate records of land grants  3. Pottery, Brahmi inscriptions and a stupa design on Socotra  4. An inscription calling Prabhavati 'mother of two kings'
Column B: a. Indian traders were present on the island over several centuries  b. A claim to supreme authority above earlier rulers  c. A system of provinces and local grants that helped tax collection  d. Her two sons ascended the Vakataka throne
questions.a: Titles reflect a claim to supreme authority; copper plates record the land grants that helped tax collection; the Socotra finds show Indian traders there over centuries; the inscription refers to her two sons who ascended the Vakataka throne.

questions.q: A province's yearly revenue is 1,500 units. The chapter says revenue paid for four things: administration, the army, temples and infrastructure, and supporting scholars and artists. In a model, 40% goes to administration, 25% to the army and 20% to temples and infrastructure. (a) What percentage and how many units remain for the fourth use, and what is it? (b) How many units go to the army?
questions.a: (a) 100 - 40 - 25 - 20 = 15%; 15% of 1,500 = 225 units; supporting scholars and artists. (b) 25% of 1,500 = 375 units.
s: Part (a): 15%, 225 units, scholars and artists
Part (b): 375 units for the army

questions.q:
A history club in Nagpur prepares a poster on Prabhavati Gupta. Card E1: her own inscription calls her a 'mother of two kings'. Card E2: she is associated with seven temples dedicated to Vishnu and his avatars, some at Ramagiri (Ramtek hill) in present-day Maharashtra. Card E3: according to some historians, her daughter built the Kevala Narasimha temple in her memory. Card E4: a modern artist's painting of her sitting in her court.
(a) Which card is not a record from her own time, and what does the chapter call it?
(b) Which strategy of the Gupta rulers does her marriage show, and what did she ensure as regent?
(c) Rank E1, E2 and E3 from firmest to least firm evidence of her importance, with a reason for the order.
(d) The poster headline can be 'A regent who kept an alliance strong' or 'A patron of Vishnu's temples'. Choose one and say what the evidence cannot show for it.
questions.a: (a) E4; the chapter calls it an artist's reimagination. (b) A matrimonial alliance; she ensured the ties between the Vakatakas and the Guptas remained strong. (c) E1 (her own inscription) is firmest; E2 follows ('associated with' is softer); E3 is least firm, resting on 'according to some historians'. (d) The political headline rests on her inscription and her regency; what it cannot show is how the alliance was kept in detail. The religious headline rests on temples only 'associated with' her; it cannot show that she personally built them. Either choice with its limit named.
s: Part (a): E4; an artist's reimagination
Part (b): matrimonial alliance; kept the Vakataka-Gupta ties strong
Part (c): E1, then E2, then E3, with a reason
Part (d): a headline chosen and what its evidence cannot show

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Gupta state.
1. Titles such as samrat and chakravartin show that the Gupta rulers had in fact conquered every earlier ruler's lands.
2. Land tax was the primary source of Gupta revenue; fines and taxes on mines, irrigation, trade and crafts were other sources.
3. Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, ruled as regent of the Gupta Empire after her husband's early death.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: the titles reflected a claim to supreme authority, not proof of conquest. Statement 3 is false: she was regent of the Vakataka kingdom, into whose royal family she had married. Statement 2 repeats the chapter.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: 'The Gupta Empire was held together by more than conquest.' Justify this using alliances, administration and titles.
questions.a: Conquest was only one strategy; the Guptas also used diplomacy and alliances such as the marriage of Prabhavati Gupta to a Vakataka prince, who later ruled as regent and kept ties strong. They divided the empire into provinces and granted land recorded on copper plates, which let local leaders share control. Titles like maharajadhiraja and chakravartin claimed supreme authority beyond earlier titles like rajan and maharaja.
s: Names conquest as one strategy and diplomacy/alliances as others
Prabhavati Gupta example
Provinces and land grants on copper plates
Titles that claimed supreme authority
Concludes why this held the empire together

questions.q: (a) A ruler of the period calls himself 'rajan'; another calls himself 'chakravartin'. Which title, going by the chapter, reflects the greater claim? (b) Why can a title by itself not prove how much power its holder really had?
questions.a: (a) 'Chakravartin'; the chapter contrasts such titles with the simpler 'rajan' and 'maharaja'. (b) The chapter says titles reflected a claim to supreme authority; a claim is not evidence of control, so other evidence such as land grants or conquests is needed.
s: Part (a): chakravartin
Part (b): a title is a claim, not proof of power

questions.q: A museum label draft on Socotra, an island in the Arabian Sea that was a stop on the way to the Mediterranean markets, has four sentences. Which sentence goes beyond what the chapter's evidence (pottery, Brahmi inscriptions, a Buddhist stupa design) supports?
questions.a: The chapter says the finds establish the presence of Indian traders over several centuries, along with traders from Egypt, Arabia, Rome and Greece. It does not say the island belonged to the Gupta Empire.
o: Socotra was governed as a province of the Gupta Empire
Indian traders were present on Socotra over several centuries
Traders from Egypt, Arabia, Rome and Greece were also there
Socotra lay in the Arabian Sea on the way to the Mediterranean

questions.q: The chapter says an empire like the Gupta had to 'promote a vibrant internal and external trade' to sustain itself. Explain why, using what the chapter says about revenue and trade.
questions.a: Revenue came from land tax and also from taxes on trade and crafts, and it paid for administration, the army, temples and scholars. Trade in textiles, spices, ivory and gemstones with the Mediterranean, Southeast Asia and China brought wealth, so more trade meant more revenue to run the empire.
s: Revenue includes taxes on trade and crafts
Revenue funds army, administration, temples and scholars
Exports and distant markets keep the empire rich

questions.q: True or False: 'When the Guptas granted land to local rulers, priests and chieftains, they lost the means to collect tax from the land.' Give the verdict, then the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the land grants were carefully inscribed on copper plates and that this system helped ensure proper tax collection, while also giving local leaders some control over their regions.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the plates kept accurate records, which helped proper tax collection

questions.q: Zara writes in her notebook: 'Prabhavati Gupta built the Kevala Narasimha temple, which shows her devotion to Vishnu.' Which correction fits the chapter's caption for this temple?
questions.a: The caption says that, according to some historians, the temple was constructed by Prabhavati Gupta's daughter in her memory. It is a contested attribution, not a settled fact, and not the work of Prabhavati herself.
o: Some historians say her daughter built it in her memory
According to some historians, her husband built it before he died
The temple was built by Chandragupta II to honour his daughter
The temple was built by the Vakataka sons she ruled for

questions.q: Write a two-line inscription for an imagined Gupta coin in which the king uses one title from the chapter. Then explain what the title claims and why a reader should not treat it as proof of actual power.
questions.a: Sample: 'Maharajadhiraja Chandra, supreme lord of kings, protector of the land.' The title claims supreme authority and superiority over earlier rulers who used simpler titles like rajan and maharaja. A title is a claim made by the ruler's side, so a historian needs other evidence, such as land grants or conquests, before accepting it as power.
s: A legend using a title from the chapter
States what the title claims
Explains why a title is a claim, not proof

questions.q: Analyse how land tax, land grants and trade worked together to run the Gupta Empire.
questions.a: Land grants to local rulers, priests and chieftains were recorded on copper plates, which helped proper tax collection. Land tax was the main revenue, with fines and taxes on mines, irrigation, trade and crafts as others. The revenue paid for administration, the army, temples and scholars. Trade with the Mediterranean, Southeast Asia and China added to the wealth, so the three parts supported each other.
s: Land grants on copper plates and tax collection
Land tax as main revenue with other sources
Uses of revenue
Trade adds wealth and links to far markets
Shows the parts working together

questions.q: Prabhavati Gupta's inscription calls her a 'mother of two kings'. (a) What does the chapter say the phrase refers to? (b) A student concludes from it that Prabhavati ruled the Gupta Empire. What in the chapter shows that the phrase does not support this?
questions.a: (a) Her two sons, who ascended the Vakataka throne. (b) She had married a prince of the Vakataka kingdom, the Guptas' southern neighbours, and ruled that kingdom as regent; the phrase speaks of Vakataka kings, not of the Gupta Empire.
s: Part (a): her two sons who ascended the Vakataka throne
Part (b): she was regent of the Vakataka kingdom, a neighbour, not of the Gupta Empire

questions.q: Tara says, 'Trade only mattered to merchants; the Gupta state lived on land tax alone.' Which fact from the chapter best answers her?
questions.a: The chapter lists taxes on trade and crafts among the sources of revenue besides land tax, and it says revenue paid for administration and the army. So the state too gained from trade. Land tax being primary does not make the others zero.
o: Taxes on trade and crafts were among the sources of Gupta revenue
Land tax was the primary source, so other sources were unimportant
The revenue was spent only on temples and scholars, not on trade
Merchants paid no tax, because the Guptas wanted exports to grow

questions.q:
A class project imagines a Gupta province whose yearly revenue is 1,000 units: land tax 700, fines 100, taxes on mines and irrigation 120, and taxes on trade and crafts 80. The governor proposes cutting the share for scholars and artists to add to the army.
(a) Does the imaginary table agree with the chapter about the primary source? What percentage is land tax?
(b) What percentage of the revenue comes from sources other than land tax?
(c) Name two other things, besides the army and scholars, on which the chapter says revenue was used.
(d) Should the share for scholars and artists be cut? Give a reason that uses the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Yes, land tax is the primary source: 700 of 1,000 is 70%. (b) 100 + 120 + 80 = 300 units, which is 30%. (c) Administration, and building temples and infrastructure. (d) Either view with a reason: cutting may help defence, but the chapter says patronage of scholars and artists was among the purposes of revenue and stability helped the growth of knowledge, so keeping it is better supported.
s: Part (a): yes, 70%
Part (b): 300 units, 30%
Part (c): administration and temples or infrastructure
Part (d): a view tied to the chapter's uses of revenue

questions.q: The caption for the Kevala Narasimha temple says that, 'according to some historians', Prabhavati Gupta's daughter built it in her memory. (a) Who built it according to the caption, and for whom? (b) Why should a student write the phrase 'according to some historians' in her notes and not drop it?
questions.a: (a) Her daughter, in memory of Prabhavati Gupta. (b) The phrase shows the attribution is a historians' view and not settled; dropping it would turn an interpretation into a certain fact.
s: Part (a): her daughter, in memory of Prabhavati
Part (b): the phrase marks an interpretation, not a settled fact

questions.q: A museum panel in Ujjayini reads: 'Varahamihira, who lived in Kusumapura around 500 CE, proposed that the Earth spins on its axis.' Which statement corrects the panel completely, going by the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says Aryabhata lived in Kusumapura and proposed the Earth's spin, and that Varahamihira lived in Ujjayini. The panel swapped the two scholars; the partial options fix only one of its two slips.
o: Aryabhata, of Kusumapura, proposed the spin; Varahamihira lived in Ujjayini
Varahamihira, of Ujjayini, proposed the spin; Aryabhata lived in Kusumapura
Aryabhata proposed the spin, but Varahamihira did live in Kusumapura
Varahamihira proposed the spin, but he lived in Ujjayini, not Kusumapura

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Gupta period was a time of constant warfare, and this is why it produced notable achievements.
Reason (R): Knowledge from previous eras was consolidated and compiled into numerous texts during the Gupta period.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The chapter credits a prolonged period of peace and stability, not constant warfare, so A is false. R is true: earlier knowledge was consolidated and compiled into many texts.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: The chapter says techniques that Aryabhata described 'were first formulated 1500 years ago' and that he lived around 500 CE. (a) Taking the textbook's year of printing as 2025, which year does '1500 years ago' give? (b) Is this consistent with 'around 500 CE', and why is the match not exact?
questions.a: (a) 2025 - 1500 = 525 CE. (b) Yes, it is consistent: 525 is within a few decades of 500, and both phrases are approximate ('around' and a round number of years), so a small gap is expected.
s: Part (a): 525 CE

questions.q: A classmate says, 'Ayurveda is only about herbal remedies.' Which part of the chapter's account of the Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas widens her view?
questions.a: The chapter says these texts deal with cataloguing and diagnosing diseases, treatments, diet, preparing medicines and surgical techniques, and that Ayurveda stresses a link between mind, body and nature. The other options attribute to them subjects that the chapter assigns elsewhere.
o: They cover diagnosis, diet, surgery and a mind-body-nature link
They give formulas for the motion of the Sun, the Moon and the planets
They deal with the planning of towns and the forecasting of weather
They record the grants of land made to priests and chieftains

questions.q: Neha says, 'The chapter proves that Kalidasa was ridiculed, worked hard and transformed his life.' Do you agree? Explain with the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says little is known about Kalidasa's life and that legends suggest he was ridiculed and worked hard. A legend is not proof. What the chapter does state firmly is his fame for Sanskrit literature and refined poetry, such as the Meghadutam.
s: Verdict: no, 'proves' over-claims
The chapter says little is known and only legends suggest it
What is firmly known: his Sanskrit literature, e.g. the Meghadutam

questions.q:
Match each description with the work or text it fits.
Column A: 1. A poem in which a banished minor deity sends a message through a cloud  2. A short treatise with formulas for the motions of the Sun, the Moon and the planets  3. An encyclopedia that ranges from weather forecasting to town planning  4. Texts compiled and given final shape on diseases, diet and surgery
Column B: a. Aryabhatiya  b. Brihat Samhita  c. Meghadutam  d. Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas
questions.a: The poem of the yaksha is the Meghadutam; the short treatise with formulas for the motions is the Aryabhatiya; the encyclopedia is the Brihat Samhita; the medical texts are the Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas.

questions.q:
A science club in Hyderabad makes a poster on Aryabhata. The modern value of the year is 365 days 5 hours 48 minutes 45 seconds. The club wants to know how a calendar using Aryabhata's year would drift over 100 years.
(a) State Aryabhata's value for the length of the year.
(b) Find the difference per year between his value and the modern one.
(c) Find the total difference over 100 years, in hours and minutes.
(d) Choose a poster headline: 'Aryabhata's year was wrong' or 'Aryabhata's year was remarkably close'. Justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) 365 days 6 hours 12 minutes 30 seconds. (b) 23 minutes 45 seconds, which is 1,425 seconds. (c) 1,425 x 100 = 142,500 seconds = 39 hours 35 minutes. (d) 'Remarkably close' is supported by the book's 'just a few minutes off' from a value found 1,500 years ago; 'wrong' can be argued from the drift of about 1 day 15 hours per century, which a calendar-maker would notice. A good answer uses both numbers.
s: Part (a): 365 d 6 h 12 min 30 s
Part (b): 23 min 45 s per year
Part (c): 39 hours 35 minutes in 100 years
Part (d): headline chosen with the numbers

questions.q: Aryabhata's year was 365 days 6 hours 12 minutes 30 seconds against the modern 365 days 5 hours 48 minutes 45 seconds. A calendar built on his year would differ from the modern value by ___ minutes after 4 years.
A historian of weather wants Gupta-age sources. (a) Name the two works in the chapter that deal with weather, and say what each does with it. (b) Why should she not use the two in the same way?
questions.a: (a) Meghadutam, the poem by Kalidasa, describes in great detail the landscapes and weather of north India along a cloud's journey; Brihat Samhita, Varahamihira's encyclopedia, covers weather forecasting. (b) The poem uses weather as part of a story in verse, while the encyclopedia treats it as a subject of observation and reasoning, so she must read the poem as literature and the encyclopedia as a work of science.
s: Part (a): Meghadutam describes weather; Brihat Samhita covers forecasting
Part (b): poem as story and literature versus encyclopedia as observation and reasoning

questions.q: 'The Gupta age was a time when old knowledge was gathered and new knowledge was added.' Justify this statement.
questions.a: Old knowledge gathered: Ayurveda, with roots going back centuries BCE, was codified in the Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas, and knowledge from previous eras was compiled into numerous texts and Puranas. New advances: Aryabhata proposed the Earth's spin, gave a close length of the year and explained eclipses; Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita covered many subjects; metallurgy progressed with the Iron Pillar. Peace and patronage made both possible.
s: Old knowledge compiled: Ayurveda and texts
New advances: Aryabhata and Varahamihira
Peace and patronage as the cause

questions.q:
Read the statements about Gupta-age scholarship.
1. Aryabhata lived in Kusumapura, near present-day Patna, around 500 CE.
2. Aryabhata's value for the length of the year is exactly the same as the modern value.
3. The Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas first created Ayurveda during the Gupta period.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 is false: his year is 365 days 6 hours 12 minutes 30 seconds against the modern 365 days 5 hours 48 minutes 45 seconds, 'just a few minutes off'. Statement 3 is false: Ayurveda has older roots, and the Gupta period codified it. Statement 1 is in the chapter.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: A teacher asks for one Gupta-age example of old knowledge being gathered and given its final shape, as opposed to a new idea being proposed. Which example fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says Ayurveda has roots going back several centuries BCE and that the Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas were compiled and given their final shape in the Gupta period. The other three are new proposals or new compositions credited to named individuals.
o: The Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas, compiled and given final shape
Aryabhata's proposal that the Earth spins on its axis, explaining day and night
Aryabhata's correct explanation of solar and lunar eclipses in his treatise
Kalidasa's composition of the Meghadutam, the Cloud Messenger

questions.q: A clinic brochure says, 'Ayurveda treats only the body and never involves surgery.' Correct both errors using the chapter.
questions.a: First, the chapter says Ayurveda emphasises holistic healing and a deep connection between mind, body and nature, so it does not treat only the body. Second, the Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas deal with surgical techniques, advanced for their time, so surgery is included.
s: Correction 1: holistic healing linking mind, body and nature
Correction 2: the Samhitas deal with surgical techniques

questions.q: Dev says, 'Gupta scholars achieved so much only because the kings paid them.' Do you agree? Explain with the chapter.
questions.a: Partly. The chapter says peace and stability strengthened the economy so the state could support scholars, artists and scientists, and that Chandragupta II's patronage enriched his court. But 'only' goes too far: the chapter also credits the work of individuals such as Aryabhata, Varahamihira and Kalidasa, and says earlier knowledge was consolidated and compiled, so the achievements had other roots as well.
s: Verdict: partly right
Patronage evidence: economy supports scholars; Chandragupta II's court
Why 'only' fails: earlier knowledge and the individuals' own work

questions.q: Ishaan says, 'A poem like the Meghadutam is useless for studying the Gupta age, because it is only a love story.' Which detail from the chapter best challenges him?
questions.a: The chapter says that apart from the emotions of love, the poem describes in great detail the landscapes and weather of north India on the cloud's journey, so it carries information a historian can use with care. The other options give the poem roles the chapter assigns to other works.
o: It describes the landscapes and weather of north India in detail
It was compiled and given its final shape in the Gupta period
It records Aryabhata's value for the length of the year in days
It lists the revenue the Gupta state collected from land each year

questions.q: Compare Aryabhata and Varahamihira and analyse how each contributed to science in the Gupta age.
questions.a: Aryabhata lived in Kusumapura around 500 CE and wrote a short treatise, the Aryabhatiya, with formulas for the motions of the Sun, Moon and planets, the spin of the Earth, the year, the size of the Earth and eclipses. Varahamihira lived in Ujjayini and wrote the encyclopedic Brihat Samhita on many subjects from astronomy to farming. Aryabhata went deep in mathematics and astronomy; Varahamihira ranged widely and combined observation with traditional knowledge.
s: Aryabhata: place and work
Aryabhata: contributions
Varahamihira: place and work
Varahamihira: range of subjects and method
Compares depth against range

questions.q:
A Pune school library has shelf space for three of these four books about the Gupta age. Book A: a poem in which a yaksha sends a message through a cloud, with landscapes and weather of north India described. Book B: an encyclopedia on astronomy, weather forecasting, town planning and farming. Book C: texts on diseases, diet, medicines and surgery. Book D: a short treatise on the Earth's spin and eclipses.
(a) Books A and B both deal with weather. Say how each treats it and which is poetry.
(b) The librarian says, 'Book D's author also wrote Book B.' Test this using the chapter.
(c) The field of Book C had older roots. How old, and what did the Gupta period do to it?
(d) One book must be left out, and the shelf should still show literature, science and medicine. Which would you leave out and what is lost?
questions.a: (a) A (Meghadutam) describes the weather of north India along the cloud's journey and is poetry; B (Brihat Samhita) covers weather forecasting. (b) Wrong: Book D is Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya and Book B is Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita; they were two scholars of the same period. (c) Roots going back several centuries BCE; the Gupta period compiled the texts and gave them their final shape (codified). (d) Leave out B or D, since both are science and the shelf keeps one science book with A (literature) and C (medicine); leaving out B loses the wide range of subjects, and leaving out D loses the Earth's spin and eclipses. Either choice needs its loss named.
s: Part (a): A describes weather in a poem; B covers forecasting
Part (b): wrong; Aryabhata wrote D and Varahamihira wrote B
Part (c): roots several centuries BCE; codified in the Gupta period
Part (d): leaves out B or D and names what is lost

questions.q: True or False: 'Aryabhata proposed that the Earth spins on its axis in order to explain solar and lunar eclipses.' Give the verdict, then the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the spin of the Earth on its axis explains the alternation of day and night. His correct explanation of solar and lunar eclipses is a separate contribution.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the spin explains day and night; eclipses were explained separately

questions.q: Rahul says, 'The Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas prove that Ayurveda began in the Gupta period.' Do you agree? Explain with the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says Ayurveda has much older roots, going back several centuries BCE. What happened in the Gupta period is that the Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas were compiled and given their final shape, that is, Ayurveda was codified.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Older roots, centuries BCE
Gupta period: texts compiled and given final shape (codified)

questions.q: (a) Name the university the Gupta rulers patronised, which the chapter mentions along with several Buddhist viharas. (b) The chapter calls the rulers' approach 'inclusive and open'. State the fact about their own faith that gives this phrase its force.
questions.a: (a) Nalanda. (b) The Gupta rulers were devout followers of Vishnu, yet they also supported other traditions, including Buddhist institutions; supporting another tradition than their own is what makes the approach inclusive.
s: Part (a): Nalanda
Part (b): they were devout Vishnu followers who still patronised Buddhist institutions

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Many key centres of art emerged during the Gupta period.
Reason (R): The Gupta rulers created a supportive environment where creativity and craftsmanship thrived.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true. The chapter itself gives the supportive environment as the setting in which creativity and craftsmanship thrived and many centres of art emerged, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A student asks why the Gupta rulers backed both a Vishnu temple at Deogarh and the Buddhist cave halls of Ajanta. Which statement best answers her, going by the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the Gupta rulers were devout followers of Vishnu but also supported other traditions and schools of thought, with an inclusive and open approach. The other options give causes that the chapter never states.
o: They followed Vishnu but supported other traditions with an open approach
They were forced by the Vakatakas to back Buddhism as well
Vishnu was worshipped by Buddhists as well, so the sites were one faith
Ajanta was carved only after the Gupta Empire had declined

questions.q: (a) Classify each cause of the Gupta decline as external or internal: the Huna attacks; the rise of powerful regional rulers. (b) Explain why the second cause could weaken the empire even without any invasion.
questions.a: (a) The Huna attacks were external; the rise of powerful regional rulers was internal. (b) It led to internal conflicts, so the rulers' control was divided from within.
s: Part (a): Huna attacks external, regional rulers internal
Part (b): powerful regional rulers led to internal conflicts that weakened control

questions.q: Of the six Gupta art sites named in the chapter's art section (Sarnath, Ajanta, Udayagiri, Deogarh, Ahichchhatra and the temple near Sanchi), the number that lie in present-day Uttar Pradesh is ___.

The Vakatakas ruled from Nandivardhana near Nagpur
The Vakatakas were a kingdom in the central part of the subcontinent
