questions.q: Show that the chapter does not let us say that the Hunas alone brought the Gupta Empire to an end.
questions.a: The chapter says the Huna tribe repeatedly attacked the empire and weakened its control over north India, which is weakening and not ending. It also says that at the same time powerful regional rulers rose and caused internal conflicts, so there was a second cause. And it closes by asking whether this was truly the end or the beginning of a turning point, so even 'end' is left open.
s: Hunas weakened control; the chapter does not say they ended the empire
A second cause: powerful regional rulers and internal conflicts
The chapter itself asks whether it was an end or a turning point

questions.q:
A Bhopal school fair has a stall called 'Why did the Gupta Empire show signs of decline by the 6th century?'. Card 1: 'The Kushana Empire weakened by the 3rd century CE.' Card 2: 'The Huna tribe from central Asia repeatedly attacked.' Card 3: 'Powerful regional rulers rose, causing internal conflicts.' Card 4: 'The Vakatakas, allies of the Guptas, ruled in the central part of the subcontinent.'
(a) Two cards do not name a cause of the decline. Identify them, with a reason for each.
(b) How many centuries separate Card 1 from the decline?
(c) Which of the remaining two causes is external and which internal?
(d) The stall can print one headline: 'Invaders at the gates' or 'Rivals within'. Choose one and state what it leaves out.
questions.a: (a) Card 1: the Kushana weakening was in the 3rd century, long before the 6th-century decline; Card 4: the Vakatakas were allies, not a cause. (b) 6 - 3 = 3 centuries. (c) Card 2 (Hunas) is external; Card 3 (regional rulers) is internal. (d) Either with its omission named: 'Invaders at the gates' leaves out the internal conflicts and the chapter's 'at the same time'; 'Rivals within' leaves out the repeated Huna attacks that weakened control over north India.
s: Part (a): Cards 1 and 4, with a reason each
Part (b): 3 centuries
Part (c): Hunas external; regional rulers internal
Part (d): a headline chosen and what it leaves out

questions.q:
Read the statements about Gupta art and decline.

2. Udayagiri and the Gupta-era temple near Sanchi are both located in Madhya Pradesh.

Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: the Ajanta Caves are in present-day Maharashtra. Statements 2 and 3 follow the chapter.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: Two terracotta river figures from Ahichchhatra have lost their lower parts, so their mounts are missing, but water still flows over their heads and each holds a pot. (a) What can a viewer still tell about the figures? (b) What can she not decide, and which detail would have settled it?
questions.a: (a) That they represent rivers, since water flows over their heads and the pot is a reminder of the rivers. (b) Which of the two is Ganga and which is Yamuna, because their vahanas distinguish them: Ganga stands on a makara and Yamuna on a tortoise.

Part (b): cannot tell Ganga from Yamuna without the vahana (makara or tortoise)

questions.q: A photograph shows a rock-cut hall at Ajanta with a central stupa from which a seated Buddha emerges; its arched roof imitates wooden beams. What does the arched roof suggest about how the cave was made?

o: The cave was carved to look like a built temple, copying wooden beams
The cave was roofed with real wooden beams brought from outside
The cave was carved as a shrine of Vishnu, the rulers' god
The cave was carved after the Huna attacks ended Gupta rule

questions.q: 'Gupta art was not limited to one religion or one place.' Justify this statement using the chapter.
questions.a: Place: Sarnath and Deogarh in Uttar Pradesh, Udayagiri and the site near Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh, Ajanta in Maharashtra, Ahichchhatra in western Uttar Pradesh. Religion: Buddha sculptures at Sarnath, a Bodhisattva painted at Ajanta, carvings of deities at Udayagiri, Vishnu on Sheshnag at Deogarh, and river goddesses in terracotta. So both many religious themes and many regions were involved.
s: Names sites in at least three places
Names Buddhist and non-Buddhist themes
Concludes

questions.q: True or False: 'Because the Gupta Empire declined under invasions and internal conflicts, the chapter treats the Gupta period as one that left no lasting influence.' Give the verdict, then the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the Gupta period's influence stretched far beyond the empire, shaping art, science, literature and governance for centuries, and that its legacy is still alive in India's culture. It even asks whether the decline was truly an end or a turning point.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the influence continued for centuries; the chapter asks whether decline was the end

questions.q:
Match each group with what the chapter says about its link to the Gupta Empire's fortunes.
Column A: 1. The Hunas  2. Powerful regional rulers  3. The Kushanas  4. The Vakatakas
Column B: a. Their empire had begun to weaken by the 3rd century CE, long before the Gupta decline  b. A fierce tribe from central Asia that repeatedly attacked  c. Allies of the Guptas who also supported Ajanta  d. Their rise led to internal conflicts
questions.a: The Hunas were the repeated attackers from central Asia; the regional rulers' rise caused internal conflicts; the Kushana Empire had weakened by the 3rd century CE; the Vakatakas were allies and supporters of Ajanta.

questions.q: Neha says, 'The art centres named in the chapter lie in at least three different present-day states.' Do you agree? Give evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. Sarnath, Deogarh and Ahichchhatra are in Uttar Pradesh (Ahichchhatra in the west); Udayagiri and the Gupta-era temple near Sanchi are in Madhya Pradesh; the Ajanta Caves are in Maharashtra. That makes three states.
s: Verdict: agrees
Uttar Pradesh sites and Madhya Pradesh sites named correctly
Maharashtra (Ajanta) named as the third state

questions.q: Among the Madhya Pradesh sculptures shown in the chapter (Fig. 7.18) is a panel of Arjuna and Karna in battle. From which text does this scene come, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The caption describes the sculpted depiction of Arjuna and Karna in battle as being from the Mahabharata. The Ramayana and the Vishnu Purana appear elsewhere in the chapter, and Jataka tales are not named in this caption.
o: The Mahabharata
The Ramayana
The Vishnu Purana
The Jataka tales

questions.q:
A Delhi school plans a three-stop study tour of Gupta art with exactly one stop in each of three states. The six sites it can choose from are Sarnath, Deogarh and Ahichchhatra (all in Uttar Pradesh), Udayagiri and the Gupta-era temple near Sanchi (both in Madhya Pradesh), and Ajanta (Maharashtra). The tour must include at least one Buddhist-theme site.
(a) How many different three-stop tours with one stop per state are possible?
(b) Does every such tour meet the Buddhist-theme rule? Explain.
(c) The students then insist on seeing the terracotta river figures. How many tours remain?
(d) The two remaining tours differ only in the Madhya Pradesh stop: Udayagiri or the Gupta-era temple near Sanchi. Choose one and state what the tour will miss.
questions.a: (a) 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 tours. (b) Yes: every tour must include Ajanta, the only Maharashtra site, which has Buddhist caves and a painted Bodhisattva, so the rule holds whichever other stops are chosen. (c) The river figures are at Ahichchhatra, the Uttar Pradesh stop, leaving 1 x 2 x 1 = 2 tours. (d) Udayagiri gives the rock-cut caves with carved deities and misses the Gupta-era temple building; the Sanchi temple gives a built temple and misses the rock-cut carving of the caves. Either choice with its loss named.
s: Part (a): 6 tours
Part (b): yes; Ajanta is always included and is Buddhist
Part (c): 2 tours (Ahichchhatra fixed)
Part (d): Udayagiri or the Sanchi temple, with what is missed

questions.q: The chapter says the Kushana Empire began to weaken by the 3rd century CE and that the Gupta Empire showed signs of decline by the 6th century. (a) How many centuries separate the two? (b) Why does this gap make the Kushanas an unlikely cause of the Gupta decline?
questions.a: (a) 6 - 3 = 3 centuries. (b) The Kushana weakening came three centuries earlier and had already set the stage for the Guptas' rise; the chapter names the Huna attacks and the rise of regional rulers as the pressures at the time of the decline.
s: Part (a): 3 centuries
Part (b): Kushana weakening was long before; the chapter names Hunas and regional rulers

questions.q: Analyse how outside attacks and events within the empire together brought the Gupta Empire to a decline by the 6th century CE.
questions.a: By the 6th century later rulers faced external invasions. The fierce Huna tribe from Central Asia repeatedly attacked and weakened control over north India. At the same time powerful regional rulers rose and caused internal conflicts. One pressure drained the empire from outside and the other split it from within, so its authority weakened. The chapter asks whether it was truly an end or a turning point.
s: Huna attacks described
Weakened control over north India
Regional rulers and internal conflicts
Shows how the two pressures combined
Notes the chapter's open question about a turning point

questions.q: Four Gupta-era works are Sarnath's Buddha sculptures, the Deogarh temple's Vishnu on Sheshnag, a sculpted Arjuna and Karna in battle from Madhya Pradesh (Fig. 7.18), and Ahichchhatra's terracotta river figures. (a) Which of the four have a Buddhist subject? (b) What does the mixture of subjects suggest about the art that Gupta rulers supported?
questions.a: (a) Only Sarnath's Buddha sculptures. (b) Gupta-era art was not limited to one tradition: it drew on Buddhist, Vishnu-related, epic and river themes, in keeping with the rulers' inclusive and open approach.
s: Part (a): only the Sarnath Buddha sculptures
Part (b): art of many traditions, not one

questions.q: Show that the Ajanta Caves cannot be called a creation of the Guptas alone. Use the dating in the Fig. 7.1 caption (2nd century BCE to about 480 CE), the Gupta period (3rd to 6th century CE) and the Fig. 7.17 caption.
questions.a: From the end of the 2nd century BCE (100 BCE) to 480 CE is about 100 + 480 = 580 years, and carving began in the 2nd century BCE, before the Gupta Empire flourished (3rd to 6th century CE). The Fig. 7.17 caption adds that the caves were carved in this period with the support of the Guptas and also of the Vakatakas. So Gupta support covers only part of the long carving, shared with the Vakatakas.
s: Works out a span of about 580 years from 100 BCE to 480 CE
Notes carving began in the 2nd century BCE, before the Gupta period
Notes the Guptas shared support with the Vakatakas, so 'alone' fails

questions.q: A student looks at the Gupta Empire's map and writes, 'The Gupta Empire ruled the Pallava kingdom in the south.' Which note under the map shows that her sentence goes further than the chapter?
questions.a: The note says the Guptas claim to have conquered parts of the east coast, down to the Pallavas, whom they may have briefly subdued. 'Claim', 'may have' and 'briefly' all hedge, so ruling the Pallava kingdom is more than the note says.
o: It says the Guptas claim a conquest of the Pallavas that may have been brief
It says the Pallavas were allies of the Guptas, just like the Vakatakas were
It says the Pallavas ruled from the Gupta capital, Pataliputra, in the north
It says the Guptas took over Kanchipuram and appointed Gupta governors there

questions.q: True or False: 'The Brahmaputra valley, which the ancient texts call Pragjyotisha, lay in the Kamarupa kingdom whose ruler Samudragupta defeated but did not take over.' Give the verdict, then the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says Kamarupa extended over the Brahmaputra valley, whose ancient name is Pragjyotisha, and that Samudragupta defeated its ruler but did not take direct control.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: Kamarupa covered the valley, and its defeated ruler was not removed

questions.q: (a) The chapter says the Pallavas appear to have been 'a tributary power' under the Satavahanas. Explain what this says about their early position. (b) Which decline gave them the chance to gain power?
questions.a: (a) They paid tribute to and were under the authority of the Satavahanas, so they were not yet independent. (b) The decline of the Satavahanas.
s: Part (a): tributary means paying tribute and subordinate to the Satavahanas
Part (b): the Satavahana decline

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Kanchipuram is often known as the 'city of a thousand temples'.
Reason (R): Kanchipuram was the capital of the Pallavas, most of whom were devotees of Vishnu.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true. R is half right: Kanchipuram was the Pallava capital, but the chapter says most of the Pallavas were devotees of Shiva, not Vishnu, so R is false as a whole.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A museum label says, 'The Pallavas founded the ghatikas that made Kanchipuram a major centre of learning.' Which rewrite stays within what the chapter says?
questions.a: The chapter calls ghatikas centres of learning that emerged during the reign of the Satavahanas, and says their establishment fostered education; it also says Kanchipuram developed as a major centre of learning. It never says the Pallavas founded them.
o: Ghatikas emerged under the Satavahanas and fostered education
The Pallavas built the first ghatikas as rock-cut caves for Shiva worship
Ghatikas were land grants the Pallavas gave to priests
The Satavahanas built Kanchipuram as their capital for the ghatikas

questions.q:
A Class 7 quiz team builds a chart from the chapter. Gupta Empire: flourished from the 3rd to the 6th century CE. Pallavas: rose to power after the Satavahanas and ruled till the latter half of the 9th century CE. Vakatakas: ruled the central subcontinent from Nandivardhana and were allies of the Guptas. Kamarupa: ruled by the Varman dynasty over the Brahmaputra valley.
(a) Counting by century numbers, by how many centuries did Pallava rule outlast the Gupta Empire's flourishing?
(b) A member says, 'The Pallavas ruled only while the Guptas flourished.' Use the chart to reject this.
(c) The poster is titled 'Who outlasted the Guptas?'. Which of the three neighbours can the chapter's facts support, and why not the others?
(d) The quiz-master must choose a question with one safe answer: 'Which neighbour ruled till the latter half of the 9th century CE?' or 'Which neighbour outlasted the Guptas?'. Choose one and explain.
questions.a: (a) 9 - 6 = 3 centuries. (b) The Pallavas are said to have ruled till the latter half of the 9th century, long after the 6th century in which the Gupta flourishing ended; they also rose after the Satavahanas, so they were not confined to the Gupta period. (c) The Pallavas, because the chapter gives their end date; it gives no end dates for the Vakatakas or Kamarupa, so it cannot support or deny that they outlasted the Guptas. (d) The first question, since the chapter names only the Pallavas with that date; the second could have more than one true answer that the chapter neither confirms nor denies.
s: Part (a): 3 centuries
Part (b): ruled till the 9th century, beyond the Gupta flourishing
Part (c): Pallavas only; no end dates are given for the others
Part (d): the first question, with the reason about unconfirmed answers

questions.q: The Gupta Empire flourished until the 6th century CE, while the Pallavas ruled until the latter half of the 9th century CE. Counting by centuries, the Pallava rule outlasted the Gupta Empire's flourishing by about ___ centuries.
Anjali writes, 'Samudragupta defeated a Pallava ruler in the south, so the Pallava kingdom became a part of the Gupta Empire ruled directly by Guptas.' Is this supported by the chapter? Explain.
questions.a: No. He defeated a Pallava ruler but did not take over the region; he let the local kings, including the Pallavas, keep their thrones as long as they accepted his rule and paid tribute. The Pallavas continued as a powerful dynasty in the south, so defeat did not mean direct rule.
s: Verdict: not supported
Defeated but did not take over the region
Kings kept thrones on accepting rule and paying tribute

questions.q: A quiz-master asks how each of three neighbouring powers stood with the Guptas. Which answer matches the chapter?
questions.a: The Vakatakas are called allies of the Guptas. The Pallava and Kamarupa rulers were defeated by Samudragupta but not taken over: they kept their thrones as long as they accepted his rule and paid tribute.
o: Vakatakas allies; Pallavas and Kamarupa defeated but kept thrones, paying tribute
Vakatakas, Pallavas and Kamarupa were all allies of the Guptas and paid no tribute
Vakatakas were a tributary power; Pallavas and Kamarupa were allies of the Guptas
Vakatakas, Pallavas and Kamarupa were all provinces ruled by Gupta governors

questions.q: The chapter says of Samudragupta's dealings with Kamarupa, 'By now, we have seen this pattern recur quite a few times.' Explain the pattern, give two examples from this chapter, and analyse why it helped the Guptas.
questions.a: Pattern: defeat a king but let him keep his throne if he accepts the ruler's authority and pays tribute. Examples: the Pallava rulers in the south and the ruler of Kamarupa in the northeast. The chapter says it helped maintain peaceful relations; tribute is part of the arrangement. A student may reasonably infer that it also spared the Guptas the cost of ruling distant regions, but the book does not say so.
s: Describes the pattern
Pallava example
Kamarupa example
Why it helped: peaceful relations and tribute (an inference about cost is credited if marked as inference)

questions.q: The Prayaga Prashasti mentions both the Pallavas and Kamarupa. (a) Who wrote the Prashasti? (b) Why should a historian look for a second source before accepting its picture of Samudragupta's campaigns in the south and the northeast?
questions.a: (a) Harisena, the court poet. (b) He wrote in praise of the king, so the Prashasti is one view from the king's own court; the chapter advises comparing multiple sources and perspectives before drawing conclusions.
s: Part (a): Harisena, the court poet
Part (b): a court poet's praise is one perspective; compare other sources

questions.q:
Match each clue with the kingdom, people or place it points to.
Column A: 1. A capital known as the 'city of a thousand temples'  2. A dynasty named Varman  3. A capital near present-day Nagpur  4. An ancient name mentioned in the Ramayana and the Mahabharata for the Brahmaputra valley
Column B: a. The Kamarupa kingdom  b. The Pallavas  c. The Vakatakas  d. Pragjyotisha
questions.a: Kanchipuram, the city of a thousand temples, was the Pallava capital; the Varman dynasty ruled Kamarupa; Nandivardhana near Nagpur was the Vakataka capital; Pragjyotisha is the ancient name of the Brahmaputra valley.

questions.q: Compare the Pallavas and the Kamarupa kingdom as centres of culture and learning, giving one similarity and two details of each.
questions.a: Similarity: both were centres of learning and culture, with temples. Pallavas: capital Kanchipuram, mostly devotees of Shiva, great patrons of art and architecture with rock-cut caves, Kanchipuram a major centre of learning. Kamarupa: Varman dynasty in the Brahmaputra valley, temples and monasteries as hubs of learning.
s: A valid similarity
Two details of the Pallavas (e.g. Kanchipuram, devotees of Shiva, rock-cut caves, centre of learning)
Two details of Kamarupa (e.g. Varman dynasty, Brahmaputra valley, temples and monasteries as hubs of learning)

questions.q: A draft says, 'The Pallavas were governors appointed by the Satavahanas who then rebelled.' Which rewrite stays within the chapter's wording?
questions.a: The chapter says the origins of the Pallavas are not clearly known, but they appear to have been a tributary power under the Satavahanas and to have gained power as the Satavahanas declined. 'Appear' is a hedge; 'governors appointed' and 'rebelled' are not in the chapter.
o: Their origins are unclear, but they appear to have been Satavahana tributaries
They were certainly a tributary power under the Satavahanas, from whom they broke away in revolt
They were Satavahana princes who set up a separate kingdom in the south
They were a Gupta tributary who rose when the Guptas declined

questions.q:
Read the statements about the south and the northeast.
1. After defeating the Pallava ruler, Samudragupta took over the region and ruled it directly through Gupta governors.
2. The Pallavas are credited with constructing rock-cut caves, and most of them were devotees of Vishnu like the Gupta rulers.
3. The Kamarupa kingdom, ruled by the Varman dynasty, extended over the Brahmaputra valley and northern parts of present-day Bengal and Bangladesh.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: Samudragupta defeated a Pallava ruler but did not take over the region. Statement 2 is false: most Pallavas were devotees of Shiva. Statement 3 repeats the chapter.
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: 'While the Guptas ruled in the north, other regions of the subcontinent were also full of cultural and intellectual vibrancy.' Justify this using the Pallavas, Kamarupa and the Vakatakas.
questions.a: The Pallavas were great patrons of art and architecture who built magnificent temples and rock-cut caves, and Kanchipuram developed as one of the major centres of learning in the south. The Kamarupa kingdom had temples and monasteries as hubs of learning. The Vakatakas ruled the central subcontinent from Nandivardhana, were allies of the Guptas and, with the Guptas, supported the carving of the Ajanta caves. So the Gupta period was one of vibrancy across the whole subcontinent.
s: Pallavas: patrons of art and architecture; temples, caves; Kanchipuram a centre of learning
Kamarupa: temples and monasteries as learning hubs
Vakatakas: central region and Ajanta support
Concludes about the subcontinent as a whole

questions.q:
A museum in Madurai has this draft for its Pallava panel: 'The Pallavas, who were all devotees of Shiva, rose to power after the Satavahanas. They founded the ghatikas that made Kanchipuram a centre of learning. Samudragupta defeated a Pallava ruler and ruled the region directly.' A Class 7 group is asked to audit the draft. The museum can print only one correction before the panel goes to the press.
(a) One word makes the first claim wrong. Which word, and what does the chapter say instead?
(b) What does the chapter say about who established the ghatikas?
(c) Correct the claim about Samudragupta using the chapter.
(d) Which of the three errors should the museum correct if it can fix only one? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 'All'; the chapter says most of the Pallavas were devotees of Shiva. (b) Ghatikas are described as centres of learning that emerged during the reign of the Satavahanas; the chapter does not say the Pallavas founded them. (c) He defeated a Pallava ruler but did not take over the region; he let local kings, including the Pallavas, keep their thrones as long as they accepted his rule and paid tribute. (d) Any choice with a reason: the claim of direct rule is the largest historical error and the one that misleads about how the Guptas dealt with the south; the 'all' and 'founded' errors are smaller.
s: Part (a): 'all'; the chapter says most
Part (b): ghatikas emerged under the Satavahanas; the Pallavas are not said to have founded them
Part (c): defeated, not taken over; kept thrones on accepting rule and paying tribute
Part (d): one error chosen with a reason

questions.q: Write three clues for a quiz whose answer is 'Kamarupa'. Each clue must use a fact from the chapter, and the three together must point only to Kamarupa.
questions.a: Any three correct clues that together fit only Kamarupa, e.g. it is mentioned in the Prayaga Prashasti; its rulers belonged to the Varman dynasty; it covered the Brahmaputra valley, present-day Assam, and northern parts of Bengal and Bangladesh; its ancient name is linked to Pragjyotisha.
s: First clue is correct and from the chapter
Second clue is correct and different
The three clues together point only to Kamarupa

questions.q: A local ruler of the Assam region claims Bhagadatta as his ancestor. (a) Which text mentions Bhagadatta, and as king of what? (b) Does the ruler's claim prove that Bhagadatta was his ancestor? Use the chapter's wording.
questions.a: (a) The Mahabharata, as king of Pragjyotisha, who fought on the side of the Kauravas. (b) No. The chapter says only that some historical rulers claimed him among their ancestors; a claim is not proof.
s: Part (a): the Mahabharata; king of Pragjyotisha
Part (b): a claim by rulers is not proof of descent

questions.q: Most of the Pallavas were devotees of Shiva, while the Gupta rulers were devout followers of Vishnu. (a) What did both ruling houses have in common as patrons, according to the chapter? (b) Why does the difference in god not make the Pallavas a poor example of cultural vibrancy in the south?
questions.a: (a) Both patronised art and architecture: the Gupta rulers created a supportive environment for art, and the Pallavas were great patrons of art and architecture. (b) The chapter's measure of vibrancy is the temples, rock-cut caves and centres of learning the Pallavas built or fostered, not which god they followed.
s: Part (a): both were patrons of art and architecture
Part (b): vibrancy rests on temples, caves and learning, not the choice of god
